definition: The supreme Jain vow of non-violence in thought, word, and deed toward all living beings. It is the first and most important Mahavrata. Ahimsa extends to microscopic life — Jains avoid root vegetables to protect uprooted organisms, boil water before drinking to kill microorganisms, and practice strict vegetarianism.
examples: Not killing insects
Avoiding root vegetables
Walking carefully to avoid stepping on creatures

definition: The doctrine of non-absolutism or many-sided reality. Truth has infinite perspectives; no single viewpoint captures the whole. Illustrated by the parable of six blind men touching an elephant — each describes a part but misses the whole. Anekantavada cultivates intellectual humility and prevents dogmatism.
examples: Listening to opposing viewpoints without dismissing
Using 'Syat' (perhaps) before making statements
Recognizing multiple religious paths can be valid

definition: Non-possession or non-attachment. The third great vow. Aparigraha means limiting desires and possessions, and ultimately renouncing all material bonds for monks. For laypeople, it means avoiding greed and excessive accumulation.
examples: Donating excess possessions
Living simply despite wealth
Not hoarding objects or relationships

definition: A worthy one — a soul that has destroyed the four Ghatiya karmas and attained Kevala Jnana (omniscience). Arhats are venerated as the first among the Panch Parmeshti. They are still embodied; after death they become Siddhas.
examples: All Tirthankaras are Arihants before becoming Siddhas
Any soul can become an Arihant through purification

definition: Destroyer of inner enemies (karma, passion, delusion). Synonymous with Arhat. An Arihant has attained omniscience while still in the physical body. After shedding remaining Aghatiya karmas at death, they become Siddhas.
examples: The 24 Tirthankaras were all Arihants
The Navkar Mantra bows to Arihants first

definition: The influx of karmic matter into the soul through activities motivated by passions. 42 channels of Asrava exist, including wrong beliefs, carelessness, and sensory activities.
examples: Lying creates karmic influx into the truth-obscuring category
Every stimulated passion draws karma like a magnet

definition: Substances that have a spatial extension. In Jainism, only Jiva and the four Ajiva dravyas (pudgala, dharma, adharma, akasha) are astikaya. Time (kala) is not astikaya.
examples: Soul has infinite spatial extension in terms of experience
Space provides the dimension for all existence

definition: Clairvoyant knowledge — one of the 5 types of knowledge. Allows perception of objects and events within certain spatial limits, often acquired through spiritual advancement or naturally by celestial beings.
examples: A monk with avadhi jnana can see distant events
Celestial beings possess avadhi jnana inherently

definition: Bondage — the actual sticking of karmic matter to the soul. Bandha has 4 dimensions: Prakriti (nature), Pradesha (quantity), Sthiti (duration), and Anubhaga (intensity). Karma bonds through yoga (activity) when kashaya (passion) is present.
examples: A passionate lie creates intense, long-lasting karmic bandha
A monk without passion produces minimal karmic bandha

definition: Devotion, specifically toward Tirthankaras, scriptures, and spiritual teachers. While Jainism emphasizes self-effort over devotional salvation, Bhakti is revered as the emotional support for spiritual practice. Bhakti combines with knowledge and conduct for complete progress.
examples: Daily temple worship is bhakti in action
Reciting stotras with devotion purifies the mind

definition: Contemplation or meditation. In Jainism, bhavana means repeatedly reflecting on spiritual truths to transform consciousness. There are 12 bhavanas prescribed for householders including impermanence, solitariness of the soul, refuge in the Three Jewels, and the futility of worldly attachments.
examples: Reflecting on mortality removes attachment
Contemplating the soul's separateness builds detachment

definition: Conduct — one of the Three Jewels (Ratnatraya). Right conduct (Samyak Charitra) is the application of right faith and right knowledge in daily life. It includes Mahavratas for monks, Anuvratas for householders, and Samitis for both.
examples: Non-violence in action is charitra
Five Mahavratas form the basis of ascetic conduct

definition: The four-month rainy season when monks cease traveling and establish themselves in one location to avoid harming rain-soaked beings (which multiply exponentially in wet ground). Chaturmas is a period of intensified study, discourse, and community practice.
examples: Monks stay at one temple for 4 months
Greater Paryushan penances happen during Chaturmas
Laypeople increase spiritual practice during this time

definition: Perception or faith — one of the Three Jewels (Ratnatraya). Samyak Darshana means right perception: unshakable conviction in the true nature of reality as taught by the Jinas. It is the foundation upon which all spiritual progress rests, like fertile soil for the seed of liberation.
examples: Believing in the soul's potential for liberation is darshana
Right faith without superstition or blind devotion

definition: Meditation — the concentrated focus of mind on a single spiritual object. Jain meditation (dhyana) is classified into four types: Arta Dhyana (painful meditation on worldly concerns), Raudra Dhyana (cruel meditation on violence), Dharma Dhyana (righteous meditation on spiritual subjects), and Shukla Dhyana (pure meditation on the soul alone). Only Dharma and Shukla Dhyana lead toward liberation.
examples: Shukla Dhyana is practiced only by advanced monks
Dharmadhyana reflects on Tirthankaras, scriptures, and religious law

definition: Substance — the fundamental category of reality in Jain metaphysics. Six dravyas exist: Jiva, Pudgala, Dharma, Adharma, Akasha, and Kala. All substances have origination, destruction, and permanence simultaneously — they are both eternal and ever-changing.
examples: Jiva (soul) is the only conscious dravya
Pudgala (matter) is the only dravya that is tangible

definition: The first disciple of a Tirthankara, who interprets and propagates the teacher's teachings. Each Tirthankara has 11 Ganadharas. The most famous is Gautama Swami, Mahavira's first disciple. Ganadharas systematize the teachings into structured doctrine.
examples: Gautama Swami compiled Mahavira's teachings
Sudharmaswami was the 5th Ganadhara

definition: The 14 stages of spiritual evolution (ladder of perfection) that a soul ascends from complete delusion to final liberation. Each stage represents a progressively purer state of being.
examples: Stage 1 is Mithyatva (wrong belief)
Stage 13 is Sayogi Kevali (omniscient with body)
Stage 14 is Ayogi Kevali (Siddha)

definition: Acharya (spiritual teacher) who has renounced worldly life and guides disciples on the path of liberation. The Guru provides scriptural knowledge, spiritual discipline, and personal example.
examples: Monks who give pravachan are gurus
Acharya Tulsi was a widely revered modern guru

definition: Conqueror — one who has conquered inner enemies (passions, delusion, attraction, aversion). Tirthankaras are also called Jinas. 'Jain' means follower of the Jina.
examples: Mahavira is called Jina Vardhamana
Jinendra means lord of conquerors

definition: Knowledge — one of the Three Jewels (Ratnatraya). Right knowledge (Samyak Jnana) means accurate, true understanding of the five substances and seven principles of reality, as taught by the omniscient teachers. It cleanses wrong perception and is attained through scripture, reflection, and meditation.
examples: Knowing the 7 Tattvas is jnana
Mati Jnana is sensory knowledge; Kevala is omniscience

definition: The canonical text recited during Paryushan detailing the biographies of Rishabhdev, Neminath, Parshvanath, and Mahavira, with special emphasis on Mahavira's life, five great vows, and conduct of monks.
examples: Read during Paryushan over 8 days
Includes the most authoritative biography of Mahavira

definition: In Jain philosophy, karma is not destiny but a physical substance (karma-pudgala) that attracts to the soul through vibrations caused by passions. The soul is pure, but vibration through action draws karmic particles which then bond. Karma determines birth, status, lifespan, feeling, and all experience. Total destruction of all karma is liberation.
examples: Good karma still binds, just pleasantly
Fasting and meditation actively destroy karma

definition: Discarding the body in meditation — a state of complete physical stillness where the practitioner withdraws consciousness from the body and focuses on the pure soul. Kayotsarga is the primary posture for both Shravakas and monks, and is essential for karmic shedding.
examples: Performed daily in Pratikramana
The posture of total physical stillness with mental awareness

definition: Omniscience — the complete and infinite knowledge attained after destroying all four Ghatiya karmas. A Kevali knows everything: past, present, future, every thought, every atom of the universe. This is the state of a Tirthankara before Nirvana.
examples: Lord Mahavira attained Kevala Jnana after 12 years of penance
Kevala Jnana is the 13th Gunasthanak for an embodied being

definition: Forgiveness — one of the supreme virtues (uttam dharma) cultivated on the spiritual path. In Jainism, Kshama is so essential that the most sacred day is Kshamavani (Samvatsari), the day of universal forgiveness. Forgiving others releases the forgiver from karmic bondage.
examples: Reciting 'Michchhami Dukkadam' seeks and grants forgiveness
Parshvanatha is celebrated for his supreme forgiveness (Kshama Vali)

definition: The 5 great vows observed by monks and nuns: 1) Total Ahimsa (non-violence), 2) Absolute Satya (truth), 3) Complete Achaurya (non-stealing), 4) Total Brahmacharya (celibacy), 5) Complete Aparigraha (non-possession). These are unqualified and uncompromising.
examples: A monk takes these for life
Laypeople practice limited versions as Anuvratas

definition: Liberation — the ultimate goal of Jainism. Moksha is the complete annihilation of all karmas (both Ghatiya and Aghatiya). The liberated soul (Siddha) rises to Siddhashila, existing in infinite knowledge, perception, bliss, and power eternally. No creator bestows moksha; it is achieved through one's own effort.
examples: Tirthankaras attained moksha at Pawapuri, Girnar, etc.
Siddhas reside in the topmost crescent of the Jain symbol

definition: An ascetic monk who has renounced all worldly attachments. Muni is a general term for Jain monks of either Digambara or Svetambara tradition. They observe Mahavratas, travel on foot, eat only from alms, and dedicate lives entirely to spiritual practice.
examples: Pujya Gurudevshri is an example of a modern muni
Sadhus take 5 Mahavratas for life

definition: Shedding of karma — the process of destroying karmic matter already bonded to the soul. Nirjara occurs through 12 types of penances (6 external, 6 internal). Conscious karma-shedding is far more effective than passive waiting for karmic fruit.
examples: Fasting destroys karma before it fruits
Pratikramana daily generates nirjara

definition: The most sacred Jain festival — an 8-day (Svetambara) or 10-day (Digambara) period of intense self-purification, scriptural study, fasting, and Pratikramana. The word means 'to stay in one place' or 'to burn past karmas'. Kshamavani (universal forgiveness) is its climax.
examples: Svetambaras read Kalpa Sutra over 8 days
Maximum spiritual effort of the year during Paryushan

definition: Returning or turning back from sin — a ritual of introspection, confession, and repentance. Daily Pratikramana (Samayika) and annual Pratikramana during Paryushan are essential practices for spiritual purification and karmic cleansing.
examples: Morning Samayika is a brief form of Pratikramana
Annual Pratikramana covers all transgressions of the year

definition: Matter — one of the 6 dravyas (substances) in Jainism. Pudgala is atomic in structure, has qualities of touch, taste, smell, and color, and can combine into larger structures. Karmic matter is a subtle form of pudgala that clings to the soul.
examples: Karma-pudgala bonds to the soul
Atoms combine into molecules through bonding and dissociation

definition: The Three Jewels of Jainism: Right Faith (Samyak Darshana), Right Knowledge (Samyak Jnana), and Right Conduct (Samyak Charitra). Together these constitute the essential path to Moksha. They are mutually reinforcing — right faith generates right knowledge, right knowledge generates right conduct, and right conduct purifies faith and knowledge.
examples: All 3 jewels together lead to liberation in this very life
Right faith without right conduct is incomplete

definition: A Jain monk or ascetic who has taken the 5 Mahavratas. Sadhus (male) and Sadhvis (female) live a life of complete renunciation, practicing non-violence, truth, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possession. They travel on foot, eat only from alms, and dedicate every moment to spiritual practice.
examples: Sadhus carry only a whisk (rajohara) and a bowl
Navkar Mantra includes salutations to all Sadhus

definition: Stoppage — the process of preventing new karmic influx. Samvara is achieved through vows, carefulness, meditation, and spiritual practices. It is the positive counterpart to Nirjara (shedding). Together they transform the soul from karmic victim to karmic master.
examples: 5 Samitis stop physical influx
3 Guptis stop mental influx
Mahavratas stop all influx for monks

definition: A lay follower or householder who follows the Jain path while maintaining family and social life. Shravakas observe the 12 Anuvratas (small vows) and practice daily Pratikramana. The term 'Shravak' means 'hearer' — one who listens to spiritual discourses.
examples: A Shravak takes 12 Shravaka vows
Shravaks support monks and study scriptures

definition: A liberated soul — a being who has destroyed all karma and attained Moksha. Siddhas reside in Siddhashila at the apex of the universe in eternal bliss. They have no body, no mind, no senses — pure consciousness infinite in knowledge, perception, bliss, and power.
examples: All 24 Tirthankaras attained Siddha-hood at their Nirvana
Infinite Siddhas exist in Siddhashila

definition: The eternal abode of liberated souls at the very summit of the universe (Loka). It is a realm of pure light, infinite space, and eternal bliss beyond birth, death, time, and change. Every liberated soul rises to Siddhashila after shedding the last karmic particles.
examples: Represented by the crescent at the top of the Jain Symbol
No return once reached — eternal permanence
